takeaway: Oesophageal carcinoma: progressive dysphagia, from solids to fluids, in an older smoker; upper two-thirds squamous, lower third adenocarcinoma.

question.text: A 75-year-old woman presents with a 4-month history of difficulty swallowing. She is now having difficulty swallowing fluids. Of note, she is a regular smoker. Select the likely diagnosis.
question.say: A seventy-five-year-old woman has had difficulty swallowing for four months. Now she has difficulty swallowing even fluids. Of note, she is a regular smoker. What is the likely diagnosis?

lines.text: She cannot even swallow her tea.
lines.say: This seventy-five-year-old woman cannot even swallow her tea.

lines.text: Progressive dysphagia: first solids, now fluids.
lines.say: Her dysphagia has grown over four months. First solids, and now even fluids get stuck.
(sigh) A tumour is clamping her food pipe tighter and tighter.
And she is a regular smoker. Tobacco and alcohol excess are linked to squamous cell carcinoma.

lines.text: Upper two-thirds: squamous. Lower third: adenocarcinoma.
lines.say: In general, cancer in the upper two-thirds is squamous cell carcinoma, and in the lower third it is adenocarcinoma.

lines.text: Remember: progressive dysphagia to fluids in a smoker is oesophageal carcinoma.
lines.say: Remember: progressive dysphagia, even to fluids, in an older smoker means oesophageal carcinoma.
